ideas.title: Grain-boundary-diffused Dy-lean NdFeB cuts heavy rare earth
ideas.technicalDescription: The 12× segmented NdFeB N42 magnets at €214.68 are the single largest cost line (44% of the whole EDU). Standard N42UH/EH grades bulk-alloy 1.5-3.5 wt% Dy to hold coercivity at the 150-180°C rotor operating window set by oil-spray cooling. Grain-boundary diffusion (GBD) paints Dy/Tb only onto the magnet surface, where the demagnetising field peaks, achieving the same Hcj with 0.6-1.0 wt% Dy — a 55-70% heavy-rare-earth reduction. At Dy2O3 275 €/kg vs NdPr 79 €/kg, and with ~11.5 kg rotor mass of which magnets are the dominant material, cutting Dy loading is the highest-leverage material move available. GBD is production-proven (Toyota, Shin-Etsu). The V-shaped buried 8-pole geometry is ideal for GBD because segments are thin (<6 mm) so diffusion reaches the core. Combine with the already-verified rotor cooling sleeve to lower peak junction magnet temperature, further de-risking the grade drop. Based on Dy2O3 at 275 €/kg and NdFeB N42 at 92 €/kg (7/3/2026 live prices).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: GBD is a post-sinter surface treatment (Dy sputter or slurry dip + vacuum diffusion anneal) added at the magnet supplier, not the EDU line — no change to rotor stacking or magnet insertion fixtures. Segment geometry, adhesive bonding and V-slot lamination pockets are unchanged, so EDU assembly cycle time is untouched. The supplier absorbs one diffusion-furnace pass per magnet lot. Incoming inspection adds a pulsed-field Hcj coercivity check per lot. Net effect: identical part envelope and interfaces, lower alloy content, no new EDU tooling.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — attacks the 61.9% rotor block at its largest sub-line via heavy-rare-earth reduction

ideas.riskNotes: Under-diffused cores risk local demag under 250 kW peak/short-circuit fault; validate Hcj margin at 180°C hotspot. ASIL-B torque security (E32) unaffected as flux linkage is preserved. NVH order-24 ripple (E33) unchanged — same magnet geometry. Rare-earth supply volatility (E35) partially mitigated by cutting Dy exposure specifically. Mitigation: retain thin GBD Tb reserve zone at pole edges; requalify short-circuit demag per sample plan below.
dfmaPrinciples: Apply performance material only where field demands it

ideas.regulatoryContext: Supports EU Battery/ELV recycled-content and critical-raw-material reduction direction by lowering heavy-rare-earth intensity.

engineering.mechanism: Coercivity Hcj is governed by the demagnetising field at the magnet surface, which peaks at pole edges. Dy raises the anisotropy field but only needs to be present in a ~100-300 µm surface shell to pin reverse-domain nucleation. Bulk alloying wastes Dy in the core where the field is low. GBD delivers equal Hcj with 55-70% less Dy on thin (<6 mm) segments where diffusion penetrates fully.
engineering.specDeltas: Magnet grade change N42UH (bulk Dy 2-3%) → GBD N42-equivalent (surface Dy/Tb, bulk <1%). Segment dimensions, 12× count, V-slot fit unchanged. Add drawing note: Hcj ≥ 1900 kA/m at 20°C, ≥ 900 kA/m at 180°C. Add pulsed-field coercivity CC.
engineering.validationPlan: Pulsed-field Hcj on 32 magnets/lot (Cpk≥1.67). Rotor-level short-circuit demag test at 180°C, 3× units, flux-linkage loss ≤2% acceptance. Back-EMF constant drift ≤1% over 300,000 km equivalent thermal cycling (E32). PPAP Level 3 on magnet PN.
engineering.dfmImplications: Zero change to EDU rotor line — same insertion fixtures, adhesive, balancing. Supplier adds one diffusion anneal + Dy coat. Incoming coercivity gate added. Part count and interfaces unchanged.
engineering.costBridge: Rotor magnet line €214.68 baseline → ~€182 proposed via ~15% material cost reduction (Dy content down 55-70%, Dy2O3 275 €/kg). Δ≈€32/unit × 200,000 = €6.4M/yr. Excludes GBD process fee (~€2-4/unit) and requal NRE.

ideas.title: Optimised V-magnet geometry cuts NdFeB mass 8-12%
ideas.technicalDescription: Beyond alloy content, the magnet mass itself (dominant portion of the 11.5 kg rotor) can be trimmed. The 8-pole V-shaped buried topology can be re-optimised with FEA to raise flux-focusing (reluctance-torque contribution) so the same 480 Nm / 250 kW is met with 8-12% less magnet volume. Techniques: deeper V-angle to lift saliency ratio (Ld/Lq), thinner outer bridge with a segmented flux barrier, and asymmetric pole spans to recover the airgap flux lost to reduced material. Because magnet cost dominates (€214.68, 44% of EDU), every gram of NdFeB removed is high-value — at N42 92 €/kg a 10% mass cut on the magnet content is worth more than most whole subassemblies. The reluctance torque increase also helps order-24 torque ripple if pole-shaping is co-optimised. This is a design lever using the existing lamination/HPDC tooling family, distinct from the GBD alloy lever, and is proven in high-saliency IPM designs (Tesla, Toyota). Based on NdFeB N42 at 92 €/kg (7/3/2026).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires new rotor lamination stamping tooling (progressive die) for the revised barrier and bridge geometry, and new magnet segment dimensions. No change to stack length, shaft interface or oil-spray cooling passages. Magnet insertion and adhesive process retained. Balancing spec unchanged. The main manufacturing consequence is one rotor-lam die set NRE amortised over 200,000/yr × 7 yr = 1.4M units — trivial per-unit. Thinner bridges raise stamping burr control requirements and may need finer die clearance.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — direct magnet mass reduction on the 44% cost line, plus inertia benefit

ideas.riskNotes: Thinner outer bridges raise mechanical stress at 16,000 rpm (E29) — validate burst margin. Reduced magnet flux risks demag headroom under field-weakening; check worst-case operating point. Torque ripple (E33, order-24) could worsen if pole-shaping not co-optimised — mitigate by coupling electromagnetic and NVH FEA. ASIL-B torque accuracy (E32) preserved via back-EMF constant re-cal. Inertia drop aids launch response (E34).

engineering.mechanism: Total torque = magnet (alignment) torque + reluctance torque ∝ (Ld−Lq)·Id·Iq. Deepening the V and tuning flux barriers raises saliency ratio Ld/Lq from ~2.5 toward ~3.5, letting reluctance torque supply more of the 480 Nm and cutting required magnet flux, hence magnet volume, ~10% at equal output. Rotor inertia J ∝ magnet radius²·mass drops, aiding launch response.

engineering.validationPlan: Overspeed burst test 3× rotors at 1.2×16,000 rpm, no bridge fracture. Locked-rotor + field-weakening demag test, flux loss ≤2%. Order-tracked NVH on 5 units: order-24 ripple ≤ baseline dB. Dyno torque accuracy ±2% for ASIL-B. PPAP L3 new rotor.
engineering.dfmImplications: One new rotor lamination die set; magnet segment dimensions change (supplier tool). Stack length, shaft, insertion fixtures unchanged. Thinner bridges demand tighter die clearance and burr control. Part count unchanged.
engineering.costBridge: Magnet line €214.68 → ~€193 via ~10% volume reduction at N42 92 €/kg. Δ≈€21/unit × 200,000 = €4.2M/yr. Die NRE ~€0.4M amortised (<€0.3/unit). Excludes NVH re-cal engineering.

ideas.title: Consolidate housing, water jacket and end-cover into one HPDC
ideas.technicalDescription: The Housing block is €47.67 (9.8%, 3 part instances, 9.8 kg), with the water-jacket housing €27.39 the largest line. Three housing part instances imply a main housing, a jacket component and an end-cover joined by fasteners and sealed by multiple O-ring/gasket interfaces — each interface exists only because two parts exist. Cast the complete structure as a single AlSi10MnMg HPDC part with an integral cast-in cooling water jacket (lost-core or drilled-and-plugged channel) and integrated drive-end bearing seat, eliminating one housing joint, one gasket set and its fasteners, and one sealing surface machining operation. This goes one level deeper than the already-verified 'cast jacket into end-cover' idea by consolidating the whole 3-piece housing group into a 2-piece (motor housing + inverter-side cover) or ideally single structure. AlSi10MnMg HPDC at A380 2,850 €/t, with T5/T7 heat treat for the 15-year salt-spray/stone-chip durability requirement. Reduces machined sealing faces, leak-test complexity and assembly stations.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a new large HPDC die (multi-slide, lost-salt-core or cast-in-channel for the jacket) — significant tooling NRE but amortised over 1.4M units. Deletes one housing casting, one gasket/O-ring set, ~6-10 fasteners and one robotic sealing/torque station. CNC machining consolidates bearing seats and coolant ports into one fixturing setup, improving concentricity and cutting a fixture change. Leak test becomes single-part. Higher casting porosity risk at the jacket wall requires vacuum-assisted HPDC and X-ray/pressure-decay QA.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €47.67 block × ~20% + DFA labour saving on ~8 fasteners/1 gasket at £38-47/hr × 200,000

NVH: consolidated housing stiffness ↑ can lower 2 kHz whine radiation (E33) — a benefit. Bearing-seat concentricity must hold for 16,000 rpm.

ideas.title: Continuous wave-wound hairpins cut weld count and copper
ideas.technicalDescription: The Windings block is €86.24 (17.7%), with the hairpin winding set €81.53 the dominant line. Conventional I-pin hairpin stators require dozens of laser-welded crown joints (typically 6-8 welds per slot pair × 48 slots = ~200+ welds), each a labour, quality and resistance-loss point. Switching to a continuous wave-wound (X-pin / continuous hairpin) architecture forms multiple turns from a single bent conductor, cutting weld joints 40-60% and reducing copper end-turn overhang length, saving 4-8% copper mass. At 800V the phase current halves versus 400V, so conductor cross-section is already modest — a continuous wave winding exploits this by using longer continuous bends without excessive springback. Fewer welds directly cuts the laser-welding station cycle time (a Germany labour-rate-sensitive operation) and lowers joint resistance, improving efficiency and reducing 2 kHz-band losses. Hairpin Cu profile at 14.5 €/kg; the 4.85 kg winding mass makes end-turn copper reduction material. Proven in Hyundai/BorgWarner and Schaeffler continuous-wave stators.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires new hairpin forming/bending tooling and a re-programmed insertion pattern, plus fewer laser-weld positions on the twist-and-weld station — reducing weld cycle time and consumable/optics wear. End-turn height reduction may allow a shorter stator stack envelope. Insulation paper and slot-fill process largely retained. The main NRE is the forming die and winding-scheme validation; the laser welder is reused with fewer shots. Copper scrap in bending must be controlled given the continuous conductor length.

ideas.riskNotes: Continuous bends risk enamel insulation cracking at tight radii — validate dielectric withstand (E29, 800V). Fewer welds lowers joint resistance but a single continuous-conductor defect can scrap a whole phase — mitigate with in-process hi-pot per phase. NVH (E33): slot-fill and end-turn geometry change can shift 2 kHz whine; re-run electromagnetic-acoustic FEA. ASIL-B (E32) unaffected (passive conductor). Springback control critical to slot fill.

At 800V, halved phase current permits longer continuous runs without excessive I²R penalty.

ideas.title: Commonise stator/housing carrier across scalable EDU length family
ideas.technicalDescription: With 200,000 units/yr over 7 years (1.4M lifetime units, E36) on a 'platform-agnostic assembly' (E1), the single highest-leverage commercial lever is a scalable EDU family: one common bore diameter, housing carrier, bearing seats, inverter interface and winding scheme, with power/torque varied only by stack length (lamination count) and cooling. This amortises the housing HPDC die, stator lamination progressive die, rotor tooling and inverter housing across multiple variants (e.g. 150 kW / 250 kW / 320 kW), converting per-variant NRE into shared tooling. The Housing (€47.67), Stator lamination (€30.63) and Power connection carrier (€11.22) parts become carry-over. This does not reduce this unit's piece price directly but slashes tooling cost per programme and lifts volume on common parts, improving supplier quoting. Proven at scale: Audi/Porsche PPE, Mercedes eATS 2.0, XPeng SEPA2.0 (~80% part sharing). This is a commonisation lever, not a substitution — savings are in amortised NRE and volume-driven piece-price leverage, not a per-part BOM delta on this variant alone.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: One flexible stator lamination die with adjustable stack-length gating; one housing die family with modular length inserts; common inverter mounting interface. The assembly line runs mixed lengths on one carrier with length-indexed fixtures. Massively reduces number of unique tools, spares, and changeover complexity. The trade is up-front architecture governance (freezing bore, bearing, interface geometry across variants) and slightly non-optimal magnetic sizing at family extremes. Common carrier lowers logistics SKUs and inventory.

ideas.title: Replace resolver with PCB inductive position sensor
ideas.technicalDescription: The Sensing block is €9.5 (2%), entirely the resolver (€9.5, bought-part price, E14). A wound resolver is a copper-and-lamination transducer needing a matched resolver-to-digital converter, precise rotor-alignment during assembly and its own signal harness. A modern PCB-based inductive position sensor (eddy-current, e.g. Melexis MLX90513 / Renesas / KMZ-class) replaces it with a stamped stator PCB and a passive copper target on the rotor, cutting part cost typically 30-50% and deleting the wound resolver's copper and lamination content while meeting ASIL-B via redundant sense coils. Inductive sensors are immune to the stray magnetic fields of the 8-pole rotor and tolerant of the oil-spray environment. They integrate onto the same PCB as other EDU electronics, deleting a connector and simplifying the harness. Though only 2% of BOM, this is a clean, low-risk bought-part substitution that also removes an assembly alignment operation. Proven: many 2023-2025 800V EDUs (Vitesco, BorgWarner) have moved resolver→inductive for ASIL-B position sensing.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Deletes the wound resolver stator/rotor pair and its RDC; adds a PCB sensor (potentially co-located on existing EDU control PCB) and a stamped copper target ring pressed onto the rotor. Removes the precise resolver electrical-zero alignment station — a meaningful assembly-time and yield gain — replacing it with a software offset calibration. One connector and short harness run deleted. PCB sensor is SMT-populated, high-volume, and cheaper at 200,000/yr. Requires EMC re-qualification of the sense interface.

ideas.riskNotes: ASIL-B torque security depends on position accuracy (E32) — inductive sensors achieve ≤0.5° with redundant coils; validate under 800V PWM EMC and 16,000 rpm (E29). Oil-spray and temperature must not detune the LC resonance — choose oil-rated sensor. NVH (E33) unaffected (sensing only). Risk: target-ring runout at high rpm — mitigate with press-fit tolerance control and n=30 accuracy PPAP.

ideas.title: Adhesive-bonded thin-gauge stator stack cuts loss and processing
ideas.technicalDescription: The Stator lamination stack is €30.63 (6.3%, single line, 12 kg — the heaviest block). Conventional interlock-cleated stacks use mechanical dimples that create short-circuit paths raising eddy losses and dictate a heavier gauge. Switching to a fully adhesive-bonded (backlack/self-bonding enamel) stack of thinner 0.20 mm M235-class silicon steel (vs typical 0.27-0.30 mm M270) reduces iron loss in the 2 kHz PWM band, allowing either efficiency gain or, at equal loss budget, a slightly shorter stack — cutting Si-steel mass. Backlack bonding also improves stack stiffness and damps the 2 kHz whine (a top-three NVH complaint, E33) by raising the stack's structural damping and eliminating the buzz of loose laminations. This is an emerging/process-change lever distinct from the family-commonisation and geometry ideas. Si-steel lam at 3.4 €/kg; a thinner-gauge, higher-grade coil offsets partly by yield. Proven: BMW, Toyota and Vitesco use backlack-bonded stacks for NVH and loss control in 800V-class motors.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a bonding oven/curing step in the stacking line and thinner-gauge coil handling (0.20 mm is more delicate — burr and camber control critical). Deletes the interlock die feature. Bonded stacks need no separate welding/cleating and produce a cleaner, quieter stack with better lamination-to-lamination insulation. Yield sensitivity to adhesive coverage requires in-line bond-quality monitoring. The stack becomes a rigid monolith easing downstream winding insertion handling.

ideas.title: Grain-boundary-diffused NdFeB cuts heavy rare-earth loading
ideas.technicalDescription: The rotor's 12× NdFeB magnet segments (€214.68, 71% of rotor cost) are the single largest cost line and a board-level supply risk. Replace the bulk-alloyed Dy/Tb magnet (typically ~2-3 wt% heavy rare earth for 180°C-class coercivity) with a grain-boundary-diffused (GBD) N42UH/EH-equivalent grade where Dy2O3/Tb4O7 is sputter/paint-diffused only along grain boundaries. GBD achieves the same intrinsic coercivity Hcj (≥1,900 kA/m at 180°C) with 50-70% less heavy rare earth because Dy concentrates at the shell where demagnetisation initiates rather than the grain core. At Dy2O3 275 €/kg and Tb4O7 1,040 €/kg, cutting HRE from ~2.5% to ~1% on 1.8 kg of magnet per rotor removes ~€2.7-3.6/rotor of HRE plus reduces price volatility exposure. NdPr backbone (79 €/kg) unchanged. This is the mainstream premium-EDU route: BMW, Toyota bZ4X and Nidec production magnets use GBD. Oil-spray rotor cooling (E30) already caps magnet temperature, so the UH class rather than EH may suffice, deepening the saving.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: No change to rotor lamination geometry, V-slot pockets or adhesive bonding — GBD magnets are a drop-in dimensional match. Supplier process adds a diffusion+anneal step but this is priced into the magnet piece price, not OEM assembly. Requires re-qualification of the magnet supplier and incoming inspection for Hcj and knee-point. Segmentation count (12×) unchanged so eddy-loss behaviour is preserved. Magnetiser fixturing and rotor balancing unaffected.

ideas.title: Flow-formed hollow rotor shaft cuts inertia and mass
ideas.technicalDescription: The rotor shaft (€61.67/pc, 3.2 kg) is the second-largest rotor line and the rotor is unsprung-adjacent rotating mass where inertia reduction is worth money for launch response (E34). Replace a machined-from-solid or gun-drilled 42CrMo4 shaft with a flow-formed hollow shaft in 27MnCrB5-2 or 42CrMo4, then friction-welded/induction-hardened at bearing journals. Flow forming (rotary flow-turning of a preform tube) produces a thin-wall (4-6 mm) hollow shaft with work-hardened surface, near-net geometry and excellent concentricity, removing ~30-40% of shaft mass and — because inertia scales with r² and mass is pulled to the outer wall — cutting polar moment of inertia disproportionately. The hollow bore also becomes the oil-spray rotor-cooling feed gallery (E30), potentially deleting a separate cooling tube. At ~3.2 kg baseline, removing ~1.0-1.2 kg of steel plus enabling the integrated oil feed is both a weight and a part-count lever. Flow-formed EV shafts are in volume production at multiple Tier-1s.

Requires a flow-forming mandrel set (tooling NRE) and a friction/laser weld station for the drive flange. Induction hardening of journals retained. Balancing tolerance tightens slightly on a thin-wall part. Net stations may reduce if the internal oil-feed tube is deleted and integrated into the bore.

ideas.title: Thinner 0.20 mm non-oriented steel cuts stator lamination cost
ideas.technicalDescription: The stator lamination stack is €30.63/pc, 12 kg (E12, E19) — the whole 6.3% stator block in one part. It is the heaviest single part in the EDU. Current premium NO steel is typically 0.27-0.35 mm M270/M330. Moving to a 0.20 mm high-silicon grade (e.g. 20JNEH1200/NO20) reduces high-frequency iron loss (which scales ~t² for eddy losses) — critical at 800V/SiC with 2 kHz PWM and high electrical frequency at 16,000 rpm (E29, E33) — but the same lamination geometry at thinner gauge does NOT save material directly (more sheets, same stack mass). The cost lever is different: thinner low-loss steel lets the design either shorten stack length for equal continuous torque (removing kg of Si-steel AND copper AND magnet), OR hold length and bank the efficiency for range. Taking the mass route, a ~5-8% stack-length reduction removes ~0.6-1.0 kg Si-steel at 3.4 €/kg and pulls proportional copper/magnet down. Bonded (backlack) lamination replaces welding/interlock to cut order-24 core-loss NVH excitation.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Thinner gauge means more laminations per stack (higher stamping stroke count) and more delicate handling, raising die wear and stamping cycle — a real cost headwind that must be offset by the shorter stack. Backlack (self-bonding) laminations cure in a heated fixture, deleting stack-welding and reducing inter-laminar shorts and NVH. Progressive-die tooling must be re-cut for the new geometry/gauge. Slot geometry unchanged so winding insertion is preserved. Requires re-lamination of the whole stator design loop with EM re-simulation.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — modest direct saving, strong efficiency/NVH co-benefit
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €2-4.5/stator net (shorter stack minus higher stamping) × 200,000; stator block €30.63

ideas.riskNotes: Shorter stack must still deliver 120 kW continuous / 480 Nm (E29) — mis-sizing risks thermal derate; validate continuous-power thermal soak. Thinner laminations are more prone to burr-induced inter-laminar shorts raising eddy loss and hotspot risk. Backlack bond-line must survive 180°C and 15-year thermal cycling (E32). NVH: verify order-24 and 2 kHz whine do not rise (E33). Higher-Si steel is more brittle — stamping crack risk.

engineering.mechanism: Eddy-current core loss P_eddy ∝ (t·f·B)²/ρ, so halving gauge from 0.35→0.20 mm cuts eddy loss ~2/3 at the high fundamental+PWM frequencies of an 800V/16,000 rpm SiC drive. Lower loss means less heat per unit torque, permitting a shorter active stack for the same 120 kW continuous — removing Si-steel, copper and magnet mass proportionally to length.
engineering.specDeltas: NO steel 0.35 mm M330 → 0.20 mm NO20/20JNEH1200; stack length −5 to −8% (12 kg→~11 kg); joining from laser-weld/interlock to backlack self-bond; slot fill and geometry retained; burr height ≤15 µm; C-5 inorganic insulation coating.
engineering.validationPlan: Epstein/single-sheet core-loss test to grade cert; continuous 120 kW thermal soak to steady-state, winding hotspot <180 °C; NVH order-track vs baseline, order-24 and 2 kHz ≤ baseline dB; inter-laminar resistance Franklin test on 10/lot; backlack peel + 180°C 3,000 h ageing. PPAP for new grade + bonding process.
engineering.dfmImplications: More laminations per stack → +15-20% stamping strokes and higher die wear (headwind). Backlack deletes weld/interlock station and its NVH-degrading shorts. New progressive die required. Shorter stack cuts stack-press cycle. Winding insertion unchanged. Handling automation must suit thinner blanks.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline stator €30.63, 12 kg. Shorter stack saves ~0.8-1.0 kg Si-steel ~€3-3.4 and deletes weld op ~€0.8, minus higher stamping cost ~€1.5-2 → net €2-4.5/stator direct; plus unpriced copper/magnet mass co-savings on the shorter machine. × 200,000 = €0.4M-€0.9M direct. Excludes die NRE ~€0.6M and downstream copper/magnet savings (separate lines).

ideas.title: Replace wound resolver with printed inductive position sensor
ideas.technicalDescription: The resolver is €9.50 (2% block, E8, E14, E24), a bought part. A classic wound variable-reluctance resolver is a copper-wound, laminated, hand-terminated component. Replace it with a PCB-based inductive angle sensor (e.g. Renesas/Microchip/onsemi eddy-current inductive resolver ASIC on a stamped/etched planar coil target), which delivers equivalent absolute-angle accuracy (±0.3-0.5° electrical) with ASIL-B/D functional-safety-rated silicon, no wound copper, and a flat PCB stator that mounts to the existing end cover. Inductive sensors are immune to stray magnetic fields (relevant to an 8-pole PMSM at 800V), tolerate 180°C, and cost less at volume because they are a PCB + ASIC rather than a precision-wound electromagnetic part. This directly supports NVH goals because a higher-resolution, low-latency angle feed sharpens field-oriented control, reducing order-24 torque ripple and PWM whine (E33). The stamped target ring mounts on the rotor shaft end with no magnet.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Swaps a wound/laminated assembly for an SMT-populated PCB and a stamped steel target — both high-volume, low-labour processes. Deletes fine-wire resolver termination and its manual soldering. The PCB stator integrates its own connector, cutting a wiring interface. Requires re-layout of the sensor pocket in the end cover and re-flash of the motor-control angle-decode. Target-ring stamping is a simple progressive die. Overall assembly labour and part complexity fall; supplier base shifts from electromechanical to semiconductor.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — small block but high-percentage part saving with NVH upside

ideas.riskNotes: Position sensing is ASIL-B torque-security-critical (E32) — must prove angle accuracy under 800V EMI, 16,000 rpm and 180°C. Inductive sensors need EMC validation against SiC switching noise; mitigate with shielded PCB layout and ASIL-rated diagnostic ASIC. Air-gap tolerance to the target ring is tighter than a resolver — fixture control needed. NVH benefit only realised if control loop is re-tuned. Requires ISO 26262 re-assessment of the sensing chain.

engineering.mechanism: An inductive sensor uses a high-frequency (~4 MHz) excitation coil and receive coils whose coupling is modulated by a passive stamped target; the ASIC demodulates absolute angle. Because sensing is inductive not magnetic, it rejects the PMSM's stray flux and needs no wound copper. Higher angular resolution and lower latency tighten FOC current phasing, cutting torque-ripple harmonics (order-24) and PWM tonal excitation.
engineering.specDeltas: Wound VR resolver → PCB inductive sensor + stamped steel target ring; accuracy ±0.5° elec; 180°C rated; ASIL-B diagnostic ASIC; integrated 4-pin connector (delete resolver flying leads); air-gap 0.5±0.15 mm; delete resolver lamination + winding part numbers.

Full PPAP for new sensor supplier.

Needs re-machined sensor pocket and control-software angle-decode reflash. Tighter target air-gap needs a locating fixture.

Inductive PCB sensor + target ring at 200k volume ~€5.5-7 fully loaded → €2.5-4/unit saved, plus deleted flying-lead termination labour ~€0.3. × 200,000 = €0.5M-€0.8M. Excludes ISO 26262 re-assessment NRE and control-software effort. Bought-part saving so unpriced by engine on the target-ring add.

ideas.title: Commonise stator diameter across scalable-length EDU family
ideas.technicalDescription: This is a platform-agnostic assembly (E1, E28) built at 200,000/yr over the programme (E36). Adopt a scalable-length EDU family: fix ONE stator/rotor lamination diameter and slot geometry, and vary only active stack length to cover the D-segment 250 kW variant plus adjacent B/C and E-segment power classes. This amortises the single most tooling-intensive items — the stator and rotor progressive-stamping dies, the winding-insertion/hairpin-forming tooling, the housing HPDC die family and the balancing/assembly line — across multiple vehicle programmes instead of one. Lamination stamping dies and hairpin bending tools are ~€1-3M NRE each; spreading them across, say, three power variants and both front/rear axle positions can double or triple effective volume on the shared tools, cutting per-unit tooling amortisation and lifting purchasing leverage on common magnets, wire and steel. This is the proven Audi PPE / Mercedes eATS 2.0 / XPeng SEPA2.0 route (80% shared) and BYD/Ford shared front-rear base. Piece price falls through volume-bracket steps on magnets and copper.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: One stamping die-set, one hairpin-form tool, one balancing programme and one housing die family serve multiple variants — variant differentiation is only stack-length spacers and end-cover length. This standardises the assembly line (single fixture set) and slashes changeover. NRE per programme drops sharply. The constraint is that a fixed diameter is a compromise: the D-segment point may be slightly off its own optimum diameter, costing a few points of active-material efficiency, traded against large tooling and purchasing savings. Common part numbers simplify logistics and inventory.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — spreads €5-10M of tooling NRE across variants and lifts commodity leverage
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Tooling NRE ~€8M amortised over 2-3× volume + 2-4% commodity bracket gain on magnet/Cu/steel

ideas.riskNotes: A fixed diameter forces the D-segment design off its EM optimum, risking a small efficiency/NVH penalty — validate order-24 ripple and 2 kHz whine on each variant (E33) so shared tooling does not degrade the top complaint driver. Cross-programme timing dependency is an organisational risk. ASIL-B torque security must be re-signed per stack length (E32). Mitigate with a diameter chosen at the volume-weighted optimum and modular stack-length validation matrix.

engineering.mechanism: Motor torque ∝ D²·L (rotor volume). Fixing D and varying L lets one lamination cross-section and slot geometry cover a torque/power range by changing only stack length — so the same stamping die, slot profile, hairpin form and winding-insertion tool serve every variant. Tooling NRE is fixed cost amortised over Σ(variant volumes); doubling shared volume halves per-unit tooling burden. Commodity price brackets step down with higher combined magnet/copper/steel purchase volume.
engineering.specDeltas: Fix stator OD and slot geometry across family; vary stack length only (e.g. 90-160 mm); common hairpin cross-section 14.5 €/kg Cu profile; common magnet segment part number; end-cover length parametrised; one balancing programme. Delete per-variant unique lamination die and hairpin tool part numbers.
engineering.validationPlan: Per-variant EM+thermal sign-off at each stack length; NVH order-track order-24 and 2 kHz whine ≤ target on 3 variants; ASIL-B torque-security re-sign per length; shared-tool Cpk≥1.33 across the length range; PPAP per variant referencing common tooling. Family DVP&R matrix rather than full re-validation each variant.
engineering.dfmImplications: One die-set/hairpin tool/balancing cell replaces N sets. Variant change = stack-length spacer + end-cover length, minimal line changeover. Common part numbers cut inventory SKUs and logistics. Slight EM compromise at each power point is the trade for amortisation.
engineering.costBridge: Not a per-part substitution — a programme lever. Baseline: dedicated tooling ~€8M NRE + single-programme commodity pricing. Proposed: same NRE over 2-3× volume (per-unit tooling burden −50-66%) + 2-4% commodity bracket gain on magnet €214.68 and copper lines. Estimated €3M-€6M programme-level. Excludes cross-programme coordination cost; not engine-priced as it is a commonisation lever.

ideas.title: Thermally conductive trickle potting replaces full VPI impregnation
ideas.technicalDescription: Stator VPI impregnation is €4.71/pc, 0.35 kg (E4, E26) — a batch vacuum-pressure impregnation process that is slow, energy-intensive and resin-hungry. For a hairpin stator (E31), the rigid formed conductors are already mechanically stable, so full-immersion VPI can be replaced by a targeted UV/thermal-cure trickle or dispense potting of only the end-winding crowns using a thermally conductive filled epoxy/silicone (e.g. alumina- or boron-nitride-filled, 1.5-3 W/m·K). This slashes resin consumption and cure cycle time versus a full VPI dip-and-bake, while the conductive filler improves end-winding-to-housing heat transfer — relevant to the 120 kW continuous rating and 2 kHz PWM thermal load (E29). Hairpin windings have far less need for slot-fill impregnation than random-wound stators because the conductors are pre-insulated and positively located, so the electrical protection role of VPI is reduced to end-turn immobilisation and moisture sealing, which selective potting delivers. Trickle/roll-through impregnation lines are proven high-volume alternatives to batch VPI.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Batch VPI (vacuum, pressure, gel, bake — often 1-2 h per batch) is replaced by an in-line trickle/dispense-and-UV/oven-cure cell with far lower resin usage and much shorter takt, enabling single-piece flow rather than batching. Removes the large VPI autoclave and its resin-reclaim system as a bottleneck. Requires validation that partial potting meets thermal-cycling, PD (partial discharge) and moisture requirements for hairpin insulation. Dispense robot and cure tunnel replace the impregnation tank — lower footprint, lower energy.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — small line but strong process-cost and takt reduction

ideas.riskNotes: Reduced impregnation could lower dielectric/PD margin and mechanical damping, risking insulation breakdown at 800V or higher NVH from less-damped end windings (E29, E33). Mitigate by proving partial-discharge inception voltage margin and thermal-cycle endurance to 180°C over 15 years (E32). Moisture ingress in salt environments must be sealed at end turns. Conductive filler sedimentation in dispense equipment needs control. Requires insulation-system re-qualification (IEC 60034-18).

engineering.mechanism: Hairpin conductors carry factory-applied enamel + slot liner insulation and are geometrically constrained, so bulk slot impregnation adds marginal dielectric value; its residual roles are end-turn immobilisation, moisture barrier and heat path. A BN/alumina-filled potting (k≈2 W/m·K vs ~0.2 for air) applied only to end-turn crowns delivers thermal and immobilisation function using ~40-60% less resin and a fraction of the cure cycle, since only the crown volume is filled and cured.
engineering.specDeltas: Full VPI dip-and-bake → selective dispense of alumina/BN-filled epoxy on end-turn crowns; resin mass 0.35→~0.18 kg; k≥1.5 W/m·K; cure UV+oven ≤6 min vs batch VPI ~90 min; retain slot-liner insulation; PDIV margin ≥1.5× peak 800V line-line.
engineering.validationPlan: Partial-discharge inception ≥1.5× peak V per IEC 60034-18; thermal cycle −40/+180 °C × 1,000; humidity 85/85 1,000 h + salt spray on end turns; surge test per IEC 60034-15; NVH end-winding modal check ≤ baseline. Insulation-system requalification + PPAP for new resin/process.
engineering.dfmImplications: Deletes batch VPI autoclave bottleneck; enables single-piece flow via dispense robot + cure tunnel. Lower resin use and energy, smaller footprint. Adds filler-handling control. Slot-liner insertion unchanged. Cycle time per stator drops sharply, raising line throughput.

Excludes dispense-cell capex ~€0.3M and insulation requalification NRE.

ideas.title: Reduce magnet mass via rotor flux-focusing geometry redesign
ideas.technicalDescription: The 12× NdFeB segments dominate at €214.68 (E9, E16) and rare-earth volatility is a board-level risk (E35). Beyond changing the magnet grade, redesign the 8-pole V-shaped buried-magnet rotor (E31) toward a higher flux-concentration geometry — a double-V or delta (triangular) IPM arrangement with optimised flux barriers — that raises air-gap flux density per kilogram of magnet by better focusing magnet flux and harvesting more reluctance torque. Reluctance torque contribution reduces the magnet volume needed for a given 480 Nm (E29): a well-designed double-V IPM can deliver 15-25% of torque from saliency, allowing magnet mass to fall ~8-12% for the same output. The rotor lamination stack (€16.78, E22) is re-cut to the new barrier geometry — a tooling change, not a new material — and the same GBD magnet segments are used but fewer/thinner. This directly attacks the largest cost line through EM design rather than metallurgy, and the added reluctance torque also gives launch-response benefit alongside the inertia lever (E34).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: The change is concentrated in a new rotor-lamination progressive-stamping die and revised magnet-insertion/bonding fixtures for the altered pocket count/shape; the stator, housing and windings are largely untouched. Fewer or smaller magnet segments simplify magnet handling and cut adhesive volume. The higher saliency demands tighter flux-barrier web tolerances (mechanical strength at 16,000 rpm vs magnetic performance), so the die and inspection must hold the bridge widths precisely. Balancing and assembly line largely carry over.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — reduces the dominant magnet line by EM redesign, magnet-price-hedged

ideas.riskNotes: Thinner flux-barrier bridges to boost saliency weaken the rotor mechanically at 16,000 rpm (E29) — burst-speed and fatigue must be re-proven (E32). More complex barrier geometry can raise order-24 torque ripple, directly hitting the top NVH complaint driver (E33) — mitigate with skew or step-skew and ripple-optimised barrier shaping. ASIL-B torque accuracy re-validated. Higher design/simulation NRE and full rotor DV cycle. Demag margin re-checked with reduced magnet volume.

engineering.mechanism: IPM torque T = (3/2)p[ψ_m·i_q + (L_d−L_q)i_d·i_q]: the second term is reluctance torque from saliency (L_q>L_d). A double-V/delta barrier geometry increases (L_q−L_d) saliency ratio, letting reluctance torque supply 15-25% of 480 Nm and cutting the magnet-flux term ψ_m required — so magnet mass drops ~8-12% for equal output. Flux focusing raises air-gap B per kg of magnet. Bridge webs trade magnetic leakage against 16,000 rpm hoop stress.
engineering.specDeltas: Single-V → double-V/delta IPM barriers; saliency ratio L_q/L_d ~1.4→~2.0; magnet mass 1.8→~1.6 kg/rotor; flux-bridge web ≥1.2 mm for burst; new rotor lamination die; step-skew 2×3° for ripple; adhesive volume reduced.
engineering.validationPlan: Spin-burst ≥1.4× 16,000 rpm on 5 rotors; rotor fatigue 10⁷ cycles at speed; demag pulse test at 180°C, <2% loss; NVH order-24 ripple ≤ baseline via dyno order-track; ASIL-B torque-accuracy map re-cal. Full rotor DVP&R + PPAP for new lamination and reduced magnet count.
engineering.dfmImplications: New rotor-lamination progressive die and revised magnet pockets; fewer/smaller segments simplify insertion and cut adhesive. Tighter bridge-width tolerance and inspection. Stator/housing/winding carry over. Balancing largely unchanged. Higher simulation/DV NRE up front.

Excludes rotor-lamination die NRE ~€1.5M and rotor DV cycle cost. Stacks with GBD idea (different mechanism).

ideas.title: Grain-boundary diffusion Dy-lean magnets cut heavy rare earth
ideas.technicalDescription: The 12× NdFeB magnet segments at €17.89/pc (€214.68, 61.9% of subassembly cost) are the board-level cost and supply risk. Baseline N42-class sintered NdFeB relies on bulk Dy/Tb (Dy₂O₃ €275/kg, Tb₄O₇ €1,040/kg) to hold coercivity at 150-180°C rotor temperatures. Switch to a grain-boundary diffusion (GBD) processed grade — e.g. N42UH-GBD — where Tb is diffused only along grain boundaries, cutting heavy-rare-earth content 40-60% for equivalent Hcj. This directly attacks the most expensive line. GBD is production-proven (Toyota, Hitachi Metals/Proterial NEOMAX). Pair with the proven oil-fed rotor sleeve cooling lever to lower peak magnet temperature ~15°C, relaxing the coercivity requirement further and permitting a lower-UH grade. Net magnet segment cost falls ~12-16%. At 200,000 units × 12 magnets this is a material saving of high magnitude with no torque or NVH penalty since remanence (Br) and thus air-gap flux are preserved. Magnet dimensions and the V-shaped buried pocket geometry are unchanged, so rotor tooling is untouched.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: GBD is a supplier-side post-sinter thermal diffusion step; incoming magnet geometry, plating (NiCuNi) and magnetiser fixtures are unchanged, so EDU rotor line and balancing operations see zero process change. Requires re-qualification of a new magnet part number and a dual-source PPAP. Segmentation count (12×) preserved for eddy-loss control. The only new validation burden is demagnetisation testing at worst-case junction temperature. No new capital on the OEM side; supplier amortises diffusion furnace across industry volume.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — attacks the single largest cost line and the top supply risk

ideas.riskNotes: Primary risk is demagnetisation margin at 180°C peak junction under short-circuit fault; mitigated by pairing with rotor oil-spray/sleeve cooling (E30) and testing Hcj at temperature. GBD magnets can show slightly lower Br scatter — control incoming with per-lot flux gate. EU Battery/ELV recycled-content and supply-security drivers favour reduced heavy-rare-earth dependence. No NVH change since Br and pole geometry preserved. ASIL-B torque security unaffected as flux linkage constant.

ideas.title: Flux-focusing V-array trims magnet mass 8-10%
ideas.technicalDescription: The 12× segment count (E16) and 1.8 kg total magnet mass drive the €214.68 line. The 8-pole V-shaped buried IPM already concentrates flux, but a re-optimised, more aggressive V-angle with thin flux-barrier bridges and a tuned pole-arc lets the same air-gap flux density be produced with 8-10% less magnet volume by improving the magnet loading factor. FEA (JMAG/Motor-CAD) redistributes the magnet cross-section so each segment does more work, trimming segment thickness ~0.4mm while holding Br·A constant. Torque density and back-EMF are preserved; order-24 torque ripple is actually reducible by shaping the pole-arc and adding step-skew, protecting the top-three NVH complaint driver (E33). This is a design lever, not a material swap, so it stacks with the GBD magnet grade change. Rotor lamination pocket geometry changes (new progressive-stamp/fineblank tool for E22), but magnet segmentation for eddy control is retained. The saving is purely reduced magnet material at €92/kg NdFeB. Requires new rotor lamination die and re-balancing validation, but no change to shaft or bearings.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: New rotor lamination stamping die reflecting revised V-pocket geometry and bridge thickness — a mid-cost tooling change (~€250-400k). Magnet segment size changes to a new part number; magnetiser fixture recut. Assembly flow (magnet insertion, adhesive bond, cure) unchanged in station count. Requires FEA-to-prototype correlation loop and re-balancing spec confirmation. Higher stamping precision on thin flux bridges raises die-wear sensitivity; specify progressive tool in high-grade tool steel.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — meaningful magnet mass cut, tooling-gated

ideas.riskNotes: Thinner flux bridges raise mechanical stress at 16,000 rpm — mandatory spin-burst and fatigue FEA to ISO validation with 1.3× overspeed margin. Aggressive V-angle can worsen torque ripple if mistuned; mitigate with pole-arc shaping and step-skew, verified on dyno order-analysis (order-24 ≤ baseline). Rotor inertia falls slightly, aiding launch response (E34). Re-balancing limits must be re-confirmed. No regulatory impact.

ideas.title: Hollow FSW rotor shaft cuts mass and inertia
ideas.technicalDescription: The rotor shaft at €61.67/pc, 3.2 kg (E18) is the second-largest single rotor line. A solid forged/turned shaft carries torque only in an outer annulus — the core is dead mass. Convert to a hollow shaft: two friction-welded (rotary friction or FSW) forged halves in 42CrMo4 (heat-treatable) with a bored central passage. For an 800V oil-spray-cooled rotor (E30), the hollow bore doubles as the oil feed gallery, deleting a separate lance. Torsional stiffness scales with the polar moment J ∝ (D⁴−d⁴); removing material near the neutral axis cuts ~25-30% mass with <8% stiffness loss at 480 Nm / 16,000 rpm. Lower rotating inertia directly improves launch response (E34), a costed customer value. Machining the hollow shaft removes turning stock, cutting cycle time and swarf. Requires a new forging/friction-weld process route and rotor-critical-speed re-analysis to keep the first bending mode clear of 16,000 rpm × pole harmonics. Bearing seats (6208/6206, E25) unchanged. Saving is material (steel removed) plus deleted oil-lance part.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: New process route: near-net forged blank halves + rotary friction welding + finish turn/grind of bearing seats. Friction welding needs weld-zone NDT (ultrasonic) and a per-lot torsion proof test. Hollow bore enables integrated oil routing, deleting a discrete lance part and its seal. Balancing is easier due to lower mass but critical-speed margin must be re-proven. Capital: friction-weld cell (~€600-900k) offset by removed lathe stock-removal time.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — mass and part deletion, capital-gated

ideas.riskNotes: Friction-weld integrity is torque-security critical (ASIL-B, E32) — mandatory 100% ultrasonic weld inspection and fatigue validation to 300,000 km / 15-year duty (E32). Hollow shaft lowers first bending natural frequency; run Campbell diagram, keep first mode ≥1.25× max operating order. Overspeed burst at 1.2×16,000 rpm required. Oil-passage cleanliness must meet bearing lubrication spec. NVH: torsional mode shift verified on rig.

ideas.title: Thin-gauge high-silicon steel cuts stator/rotor iron loss and mass
ideas.technicalDescription: Stator lamination stack €30.63/pc @ 12 kg (E19) and rotor lamination stack €16.78/pc @ 6.5 kg (E22) together are ~€47/unit of Si-steel (Si Steel Lam €3.4/kg). Baseline is presumably M270-35A class 0.35mm. For an 800V SiC drive running higher PWM (2 kHz whine, E33) and 16,000 rpm, iron loss scales strongly with frequency and gauge. Switch to a thinner 0.27mm or 0.25mm high-silicon grade (e.g. NO20/M250-27 class, ~3.2% Si) with lower core loss. Thinner gauge reduces eddy-current loss (∝ t²), permitting a marginally shorter stack for equal thermal budget — trimming iron mass ~5-8% and cutting the 2 kHz loss-driven whine excitation. This is a grade+gauge lever on two lines at once. Slot fill and winding geometry unchanged, so hairpin tooling untouched. Stamping die must handle thinner strip (more strokes per stack, higher burr control), and the interlock/bonding of thinner laminations needs process confirmation. Net: modest material saving plus efficiency gain that supports downsizing elsewhere.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Thinner strip means more laminations per stack — higher stamping stroke count and press throughput demand, plus tighter burr and interlock control (consider laser-cut or bonded lamination for prototypes). Coating adhesion (C5/C6 insulation) re-qualified. Stack height tolerance re-set. Same slot geometry keeps hairpin insertion fixtures unchanged. Die refresh for thinner gauge (~€200-300k). Scrap/edge-trim yield monitored. VPI impregnation (E26) unaffected.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — two lines, efficiency co-benefit

ideas.riskNotes: Thinner high-Si steel is more brittle — stamping burr and edge-fracture risk; mitigate with tuned die clearance and post-anneal. Core-loss and NVH gains must be dyno-verified: 2 kHz PWM whine sound-power ≤ baseline (E33), efficiency map re-mapped. Thermal margin at 120 kW continuous re-checked if stack shortened. Interlock strength for 16,000 rpm rotor stack fatigue-validated. No regulatory impact.

ideas.title: HPDC AlSi10MnMg housing integrates end cover, deletes joints
ideas.technicalDescription: Housing water jacket €27.39 (E20, 6.2 kg) plus End cover DE/NDE €10.14×2 = €20.28 (E21, 3.6 kg) are €47.67 across the Housing subassembly (E11, 9.8%). Baseline is a separate cast/machined housing plus two bolted end covers with sealing interfaces. Consolidate the NDE end cover into the housing as a single high-pressure die-cast (HPDC) AlSi10MnMg shell with the cooling water jacket cored in (per the proven integrated-jacket lever), leaving only the DE cover removable for rotor/bearing assembly. This deletes one cover part, its O-ring/gasket, ~8-12 bolts and one sealing interface — killing a leak path and an assembly station. HPDC in AlSi10MnMg (2,850 €/t A380-class) gives net-shape walls ~3mm, reducing machining stock. Salt-spray/stone-chip durability (E32) is aided by fewer joints. Wall sections tuned for the water-jacket pressure and stiffness (∝ t³) to hold NVH — housing radiated noise is a stiffness function, protecting the 2 kHz whine target (E33). Requires a new HPDC die and casting-porosity validation for the pressurised jacket.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Replaces two castings + machining + bolted assembly with one larger HPDC casting plus one remaining DE cover. New die is significant capital (~€1.5-2.5M) but amortised over 200,000/yr × 7yr = 1.4M parts. Deletes ~10 bolts, one gasket, one leak-test station per unit; retains a single machined sealing face. Porosity control (vacuum-assisted HPDC) required for water-jacket integrity. Machining fixtures simplified to one datum. Assembly DFA time drops materially.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: deleted cover €10.14 + fasteners/seal/labour ~€3 − casting complexity add ≈ €7-10/unit × 200,000

Casting large integrated part raises scrap/porosity risk; mitigate with process-window DOE and X-ray sampling. Removing a joint reduces leak paths (durability positive). Housing stiffness/NVH re-verified: modal frequencies ≥ baseline, 2 kHz whine radiated noise ≤ baseline (E33). REACH-compliant Cr-free coating on Al. E-coat/passivation for salt-spray.

ideas.title: Commonise stator diameter across scalable EDU family
ideas.technicalDescription: Every priced line here — magnets (E16), hairpin set (E17), lamination stacks (E19/E22), housing (E20/E21) — carries per-variant NRE and low-volume tooling burden. Adopt the proven scalable-length EDU family principle: fix ONE stator/rotor bore diameter and vary only stack length to cover the D-segment 250 kW variant plus adjacent power classes, running all variants on shared lamination dies, hairpin forming tooling, and housing HPDC die (only the axial length insert changes). This is a commonisation lever, not a part change: it amortises the expensive stamping and casting tooling across far more than 200,000 units/yr, and lets the hairpin set (E17, €81.53) and lamination stacks buy at higher combined volume, dropping piece price via scale. Magnet segment (E16) buys as a common part number across variants, strengthening supply leverage against rare-earth volatility (E35). Estimated 5-9% piece-price reduction on the tooled lines from volume consolidation and NRE amortisation. No physics change to the 250 kW variant itself; validation is carry-over plus delta-length verification per derivative.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Shared bore diameter means one lamination blanking die footprint with length-programmable stacking, one hairpin forming/bending cell with variable conductor count, and one housing HPDC die with an axial-length insert. Cuts distinct part numbers, spares, and changeover complexity. Higher combined line volume improves OEE and supplier pricing. Requires up-front platform engineering discipline and a governance freeze on the common diameter. Per-variant validation reduces to delta testing.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — amortises the most expensive tooling across the family
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: ~€130/unit tooled-line content × ~5-7% scale/NRE benefit × 200,000, plus cross-variant NRE avoidance

ideas.riskNotes: Commonisation risk is over-constraining the diameter so a future high-torque variant is compromised — mitigate by choosing the bore at the family torque-density optimum and varying stack length. NVH signatures differ per stack length; each derivative needs its own order-24 and 2 kHz whine sign-off (E33). No single-variant durability risk since this variant's physics is unchanged. Supply consolidation on common magnet PN reduces rare-earth exposure (E35). Not expressible as a single-part engine check.

ideas.title: Inductive PCB position sensor replaces VR resolver
ideas.technicalDescription: The Resolver at €9.5/pc (E24, bought-part, Sensing 2% E14) is a classic variable-reluctance (VR) resolver: a wound stator/rotor sensor requiring precise mechanical alignment, dedicated resolver-to-digital conversion, and shielded wiring. Replace with a contactless inductive position sensor (PCB-based, e.g. Renesas/Melexis IPS or Microchip LX3302-class) — a printed planar coil PCB with a stamped coupler target on the shaft. These deliver equivalent or better angular accuracy for FOC and ASIL-B torque security (E32) at roughly 40-55% of a VR resolver's installed cost, with lower mass, no wound components, and simpler mounting tolerance. For an 800V SiC drive the inductive sensor's immunity and higher bandwidth also help suppress PWM-related position error that feeds order-24 torque ripple (E33). Being a bought-part swap, the saving is a supplier price delta, not an engine-costed process change. Deletes the resolver's shielded harness and RDC front-end complexity. Requires re-qualification of the position feedback loop for functional safety and EMC in the 800V/SiC environment.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Swaps a wound electromechanical sensor for a PCB assembly plus a stamped steel coupler — fewer alignment-critical parts, simpler press-fit mounting, lower reject rate. Deletes the resolver excitation/RDC channel, simplifying the control PCB and harness. Assembly tolerance window widens (inductive sensors tolerate more axial/radial runout). Requires EMC re-test in the SiC switching environment and ASIL-B safety re-certification of the position path. Supplier tooling for the PCB and coupler is modest.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — small line, but clean bought-part saving

ideas.riskNotes: Position sensing is ASIL-B safety-critical (E32) — full functional-safety re-certification of the feedback path and worst-case angular-error budget required. EMC robustness in high-dv/dt SiC 800V environment must be proven (E29); inductive sensors are generally robust but need shielding validation. Torque-ripple/NVH: verify order-24 ripple ≤ baseline with new sensor latency (E33). Temperature drift over −40 to +160°C characterised. Dual-source the sensor to de-risk single supplier.

ideas.title: Stamped flat-copper busbar replaces round-bar phase connections
ideas.technicalDescription: Phase busbar €3.74/pc × 3 = €11.22 (E13/E23, 0.66 kg, Hairpin Cu Profile 14.5 €/kg). At 800V the phase current halves versus a 400V unit for the same power (E29), so the required copper cross-section is smaller than a legacy carry-over busbar may reflect. Re-optimise the three phase busbars as stamped-and-formed flat OFHC copper (C11000) sized to the true 800V current density (~4-5 A/mm² with the water-jacket cooling), trimming copper mass ~15-20%, then join to the hairpin phase leads by laser welding rather than bolted lugs. Flat stamped busbars nest efficiently on a progressive die (high material utilisation), and laser-welded terminations delete bolts, washers and a torque operation while lowering joint resistance (less I²R loss). This is a gauge/section-reduction plus process lever on a small but fully-costed line. Copper saving scales with the 15-20% section cut × €11.7/kg. Requires current-density and thermal validation at 120 kW continuous plus busbar isolation/creepage re-check for 800V.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Progressive-die stamping of flat copper with high strip utilisation replaces machined/bent round bar, cutting scrap and piece price. Laser-welded terminations to hairpin leads delete bolted lugs, torque control and re-torque warranty risk, and shorten assembly cycle. Requires weld-quality monitoring (resistance/peel per sample) and busbar overmould or coating for 800V isolation and creepage. New stamping tool (~€150-250k). Insulation coordination re-verified.

ideas.riskNotes: 800V insulation coordination is safety-critical: creepage/clearance and partial-discharge re-qualified per the DC-link voltage (E29). Reduced section must hold thermal at 120 kW continuous — thermal-rise test with acceptance ≤ insulation class limit. Laser-welded copper joints need per-lot destructive peel sampling for ASIL-B current integrity (E32). Overmould material must survive salt-spray/temperature. Skin effect at 2 kHz negligible at these sections but confirmed.
